nameStory: The pointed campeloma gets its name from its distinctively sharp, pointed spire that tapers to a fine tip. The genus name 'Campeloma' comes from Greek words meaning 'curved border,' referring to the elegant curves of the shell's opening.
description: The pointed campeloma is a freshwater snail that lives underwater in New England's rivers, streams, and lakes. This aquatic snail carries a spiral shell that's typically brown or olive-colored and comes to a sharp point at the top. Like other river snails, it has a trapdoor-like structure called an operculum that can seal shut when the snail retreats into its shell. These snails are live-bearers, meaning they give birth to tiny, fully-formed baby snails rather than laying eggs.

idTips.label: Pointed spire
idTips.description: The shell tapers to a distinctly sharp, needle-like point at the top, much more pronounced than most other freshwater snails you'll encounter

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: The shell feels smooth when dry, with a slightly glossy surface that may have fine growth lines you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Typically brown to olive-brown coloration, sometimes with darker bands or streaks running along the whorls of the shell

idTips.label: Operculum door
idTips.description: Look for the dark, oval-shaped trapdoor that covers the shell opening when the snail is retracted - it feels firm and slightly horn-like

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: The shell is cone-shaped with 5-7 whorls that gradually increase in size toward the bottom, creating a classic spiral snail silhouette

habitat: Pointed campelomas prefer slow-moving or still freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, quiet river backwaters, and stream pools with muddy or sandy bottoms. They're often found in areas with aquatic vegetation where they can graze on algae and organic matter. Look for them in shallow water areas along the edges of water bodies where sediment has accumulated.

seasonality.spring: Snails become more active as water warms, making them easier to spot crawling on submerged surfaces or in shallow water near shorelines.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most visible and actively feeding. This is the best time to observe them moving around and to find fresh, undamaged shells.
seasonality.fall: Activity slows as temperatures drop, but shells can still be found along shorelines. Empty shells may wash up on beaches after autumn storms.
seasonality.winter: Snails retreat to deeper water and become largely inactive. Look for empty shells in lake ice or washed up along winter shorelines.

funFact: Pointed campelomas are living pregnancy champions - females can carry developing babies for nearly a year before giving birth to tiny, perfectly formed snails that are ready to start life immediately without any helpless larval stage!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other freshwater snails, but the pointed campeloma's sharp, needle-like spire is much more pronounced than the rounded or blunt tops of most other species. Remember: if it looks like it could poke you, it's probably a pointed campeloma!
contextualKnowledge: The term 'operculum' might sound fancy, but it's just the scientific name for the snail's natural door - think of it as a built-in turtle shell that seals the opening. Many people don't realize that freshwater snails like this one breathe through gills underwater, unlike their land snail cousins that use lungs.
compareHints: Since pointed campeloma is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other river snails in the same family. Unlike the more rounded river snails, pointed campelomas have that distinctive sharp spire that really sets them apart. Other viviparid snails in the region tend to have more globular, rounded shells without such a pronounced point.
